Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
revision_notes: Cited source fetched and confirmed: TheGlobalEconomy.com, citing ITU, gives Angola's international internet bandwidth per internet user as 3.37 kbit/s, dated 2015 (data availability window 2012-2015), well within the <5 kbit/s 'Very Low' band, so Value Code 1 is supported by the cited evidence. No fresher ITU-published per-user bandwidth figure could be located despite searching ITU DataHub and related trackers -- ITU appears not to have reported this indicator for Angola since 2015. A secondary, non-ITU aggregator (USAID mAccess Diagnostic Tool, published 2023) lists an 'international bandwidth per user' value of 8.80 for Angola, but the unit (kbit/s vs Mbit/s) is not stated on the page and could not be confirmed, so this was not used to change the score. Angola has since added substantial submarine cable capacity (SACS live 2018, WACS since 2012, 2Africa/Equiano landing 2023-2025), which makes it plausible that per-user bandwidth has risen materially since 2015, but without a dated, unit-confirmed authoritative figure this cannot be quantified. Score confirmed as the best-evidenced figure available, but flagged given the 11-year vintage of the only clear ITU data point and the unverified higher secondary estimate.
revised_comments: Angola's international internet bandwidth per internet user is very low. The most recent internationally comparable figure, an ITU-sourced estimate reported via TheGlobalEconomy.com, puts it at 3.37 kbit/s per user, dating from 2015, the last year for which ITU published a value for this indicator for Angola. This sits well below the 5 kbit/s threshold for the lowest band on this measure. Angola has expanded its international connectivity substantially since then through submarine cable systems including WACS, SACS and, more recently, 2Africa and Equiano, but no updated, authoritative per-user bandwidth figure is publicly available to quantify the effect of this expansion.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
revision_notes: Cited source fetched and confirmed: Afrobarometer's 2023 Angola survey (AD664) reports 92% of urban residents living in zones served by the national electricity grid versus 14% of rural residents, a gap of roughly 78 percentage points, matching the figures already recorded in Comments. This is corroborated by World Bank/ESMAP Tracking SDG7 data (published 2023, most recent year 2023): national access to electricity is 51.1% while urban access is 77.9%, implying a much lower rural rate consistent with a gap well over 60 percentage points (a full rural World Bank figure for 2023 could not be retrieved directly, but the 2018 rural figure of 7.33% and the large urban-national gap both point the same direction). Both independent sources place the gap firmly in the '>60 percentage points' band, so Value Code 1 is confirmed.
revised_comments: Angola has a wide urban-rural electrification gap. Afrobarometer's 2023 survey finds that 92% of urban residents live in areas served by the national electricity grid, compared with just 14% of rural residents, a gap of around 78 percentage points. This is corroborated by World Bank/ESMAP Tracking SDG7 data for 2023, which record overall access to electricity at 51.1% of the population against 77.9% in urban areas, implying a much lower rural access rate. The gap comfortably exceeds 60 percentage points.
